peace.e: From Middle English pees, pes, pais, borrowed from Anglo-Norman peis and Old French pais (“peace”), from Latin pāx (“peace”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ḱ- (“to fasten, stick, place”), related to Latin pacīscor (“agree, stipulate”), Latin pangō (“fasten, fix”); see pact.
peace.g: A state of tranquility, quiet, and harmony. For instance, a state free from civil disturbance.

peaceable.e: From Anglo-Norman pesible, peisible, Middle French paisible, from pais (“peace”) + -ible; later remodelled after peace + -able.
peaceable.g: Favouring peace rather than conflict; not aggressive, tending to avoid violence (of people, actions etc.).

peaceably.e: From Middle English pesibly; equivalent to peaceable + -ly.

peaceful.e: From Middle English peesful, pesful, paisful, pesefull. By surface analysis, peace + -ful.
peaceful.g: Not at war; not disturbed by strife or turmoil.

peaceful.e: From the derogatory term religion of peace, which is used against Islam itself for its association with violent attacks by Islamic extremists, and alleged support and lack of condemnation against them by certain Muslim communities.
peaceful.g: A non-player character who is not hostile to the player.

peacemaker.g: A person who restores peace, especially by settling disputes; one who engages in peacemaking.

peacetime.g: The period of time when a nation or people is at peace, not fighting a war.

peacock.e: From Middle English pecok, pekok, pocok, pacok, first component from Old English pēa, pāwa (“peacock, peafowl”), ultimately from Latin pāvō; equivalent to pea + cock.
peacock.g: A male peafowl, especially Pavo cristatus, notable for its brilliant iridescently ocellated tail.

peak.e: From earlier peake, peek, peke, from Middle English pek (in place names), itself an alteration of pike, pyke, pyk (“a sharp point, pike”), from Old English pīc, piic (“a pike, needle, pin, peak, pinnacle”), from Proto-West Germanic *pīk, from Proto-Germanic *pīkaz (“peak”).
peak.g: A point; the sharp end or top of anything that terminates in a point; as, the peak, or front, of a cap.

peak.e: Unknown. Perhaps related to Etymology 1 above in the sense of "becoming pointed" through emaciation.

peal.e: From Middle English pele, peil, probably an apheretic variant of Middle English apel, appel, from Old French apel (“an appeal; pealing of bells”).
peal.g: A loud sound, or a succession of loud sounds, as of bells, thunder, cannon, shouts, laughter, of a multitude, etc.

pearl.e: From Middle English perle, from Old French perle of uncertain etymology. Probably via unattested Medieval Latin *pernula, from Latin perna (“haunch; a marine bivalve shaped like a leg of lamb”) but also derived from Medieval Latin perla, from Latin perula (“little bag”).
pearl.g: A shelly concretion, usually rounded, and having a brilliant luster, with varying tints, found in the mantle, or between the mantle and shel

pebble.e: From Middle English pibel (also in pibleston), from Old English papolstān (“pebble-stone”), from Old English *papol, *pyppel, *pæbbel of unknown origin + Old English stān.
pebble.g: A small stone, especially one rounded by the action of water.

peculiar.e: From Latin pecūliāris (“one's own”), from pecūlium (“private property”), from pecus (“cattle”).
peculiar.g: Out of the ordinary; odd; strange; unusual.

peddle.e: Back-formation from pedlar. (Compare burgle from burglar.)
peddle.g: To sell things, especially door to door or in insignificant quantities.

pedestal.e: Borrowed from Middle French piédestal, itself borrowed from Italian piedistallo (literally “foot stand”). Spelling influenced by Latin pēs, pedem.
pedestal.g: The base or foot of a column, statue, vase, lamp.

pedigree.e: From Anglo-Norman pé de grue, a variant of Old French pié de gru (“foot of a crane”), from Latin pes (“foot”) + grus (“crane”).
pedigree.g: A chart, list, or record of ancestors, to show breeding, especially distinguished breeding.

peel.e: From Middle English pelen, from Old English pilian and Old French peler, pellier; both from Latin pilō, pilāre (“to remove hair from, depilate”), from pilus (“hair”).
peel.g: To remove the skin or outer covering of.

peel.e: From Middle English peel, pele, from Anglo-Norman pel (compare modern French pieu), from Latin pālus (“stake”).

peeled.g: With the outermost layer or skin removed.

peep.g: A short, soft, high-pitched sound, as made by a baby bird.
A spot on a die or domino.

peer.e: From Middle English peren, pyren, piren (“to peer, gaze”), perhaps from Old English *pȳran (“to look, peer”), from Proto-West Germanic *pūrijan (“to look”), related to Saterland Frisian pierje (“to look”), Dutch Low Saxon piren (“to look”), West Flemish pieren (“to look with narrowed eyes, squint at”), Dutch pieren (“to look closely at, examine”).
peer.g: To look with difficulty, or as if searching for something.

peer.e: From Middle English per, pere, from Anglo-Norman peir, Old French per, from Latin pār.
peer.g: Somebody who is, or something that is, at a level or of a value equal (to that of something else).

peg.e: From Middle English pegge, from Middle Dutch pegge (“pin, peg”), from Old Dutch *pigg-, *pegg-, from Proto-Germanic *pig-, *pag- (“peg, stake”), from Proto-Indo-European *bak-, *baḱ- (“club, pointed stick, peg”). This is one of the very few English words that begin with a p and come from Proto-Germanic.
peg.g: A cylindrical wooden or metal object used to fasten or as a bearing between objects.

pelican.e: From Middle English pellican, pellicane, from Old English pellican (“pelican”), from Latin pelecānus, from Ancient Greek πελεκάν (pelekán), πέλεκυς (pélekus, “hatchet”).
pelican.g: Any of various seabirds of the family Pelecanidae, having a long bill with a distendable pouch.

pelt.e: Uncertain; possibly related to pelting (“mean, paltry”) (obsolete), peltry (“rubbish, trash; an unpleasant thing”) (chiefly Scotland, obsolete), and paltry (“of little value, trashy, trivial; contemptibly unimportant, despicable”), possibly from a Germanic language such as Middle Low German palte, palter (“cloth; rag, shred”).
pelt.g: A tattered or worthless piece of clothing; a rag.

pelt.e: Uncertain; possibly related to palter (“to talk insincerely; to prevaricate or equivocate in speech or actions; to haggle; to babble, chatter; (rare) to trifle”), further etymology unknown. The Oxford English Dictionary takes the view that any relation to pelting (“mean, paltry”) (obsolete) and paltry (“of little value, trashy, trivial.
pelt.g: To bargain for a better deal; to haggle.

pen.e: By incorrect analogy with man → men.

penalty.e: From Middle French pénalité, from pénal, from Latin poenālis, from poena, borrowing of Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ), from Proto-Hellenic *kʷoinā́, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷoynéh₂, comprising *kʷey- + *-néh₂.

pendant.e: From Anglo-Norman pendaunt, Middle French pendant, noun use of adjective.
pendant.g: A supporting post attached to the main rafter.

penknife.e: From Middle English penne knyfe; equivalent to pen + knife. In the original sense, named for its purpose: aiding the use of a (traditional) ink pen through the following tasks: trimming the tip of a quill pen, trimming a reed for a nib, and (in some cases) allowing erasure by scraping away some ink.

penny.e: From Middle English peny, from Old English peniġ, penniġ, penning (“penny”), from Proto-West Germanic *panning, from Proto-Germanic *panningaz, of uncertain origin (see that page for theories).
penny.g: In the United Kingdom and Ireland and many other countries, a unit of currency worth ¹⁄₂₄₀ of a pound sterling or Irish pound before decimal

pennyworth.g: The amount that can be bought for a penny.

penury.e: From Late Middle English penuri, penurie (“destitution, need, poverty; dearth, lack, scarcity”), borrowed from Latin pēnūria (“need, scarcity, want”) + Middle English -i, -ie (suffix forming abstract and collective nouns); further etymology uncertain, possibly related to paene (“almost, nearly.
penury.g: Extreme need or want; destitution, poverty; (countable) an instance of this.

people.e: From Middle English puple, peple, peeple, from Anglo-Norman people, from Old French pueple, peuple, pople, from Latin populus (“a people, nation”), from Old Latin populus, from earlier poplus, from even earlier poplos, from Proto-Italic *poplos (“army”) of unknown origin. Gradually ousted native English lede and, partially, folk.
people.g: To interact with people; to socialize.

per.e: From Latin per (“through, during”), from Proto-Indo-European *per.
Clipping of person, coined by American novelist and poet Marge Piercy in Woman on the Edge of Time (1979)
per.g: They (singular). Gender-neutral neologistic third-person singular subject pronoun, coordinate with gendered pronouns he and she.

peradventure.e: From Middle English peraventure, peradventure, from Old French par aventure. Spelling modified as though from Latin. Equivalent to per- + adventure.

perceive.e: From Middle English perceyven, borrowed from Old French percevoir, perceveir, from Latin percipiō, past participle perceptus (“take hold of, obtain, receive, observe”), from per (“by, through”) + capiō (“to take”); see capable.
perceive.g: To become aware of, through the physical senses, to see; to understand.

percentage.e: From percent, from Latin per centum (“for every hundred”), + -age (suffix indicating a rate).
percentage.g: The amount, number or rate of something, regarded as part of a total of 100; a part of a whole.

perch.e: From Middle English perche, from Old French perche, from Latin perca, from Ancient Greek πέρκη (pérkē, “perch”), cognate with περκνός (perknós, “dark-spotted”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *perḱ-, whence also Old English forn (“trout”), German Forelle (“trout”).
perch.g: Any of the three species of spiny-finned freshwater fish in the genus Perca.

perch.e: From Middle English perche, from Old French perche, from Latin pertica (“staff, long pole, measuring rod”).
perch.g: A rod, staff, tree branch, ledge, etc., used as a roost by a bird.

perdition.e: From Middle English perdicioun, from Old French perdiciun, from Late Latin perditio, from Latin perdo (“to destroy, to lose”).

perfect.e: From Middle English perfit, from Old French parfit (modern: parfait), from Latin perfectus, perfect passive participle of perficere (“to finish”), from per- (“through, thorough”) + facere (“to do, to make”). The spelling was modified in the 15th century to conform to its Latin etymon.

perfect.g: To make perfect; to improve or hone.

perfection.e: From Middle English perfeccioun, from Old French perfection, from Latin perfectiō. By surface analysis, perfect + -ion.
perfection.g: The quality or state of being perfect or complete, so that nothing substandard remains; the highest attainable state or degree of excellence

perfectness.e: From Middle English parfitnesse; equivalent to perfect + -ness.
perfectness.g: The quality of being perfect; perfection.

perform.e: From Middle English parformen, performen (“to perform”), from Anglo-Norman performer, parfourmer, alteration of Old French parfornir, parfurnir (“to complete, accomplish, perform”), from par- + fornir, furnir (“to accomplish, furnish”), from Frankish *frummjan (“to accomplish, furnish”), from Proto-Germanic *frumjaną, *framjaną (“to further, promote”).

performance.e: From Middle English parfourmaunce; equivalent to perform + -ance.
performance.g: The act of performing; carrying into execution or action; execution; achievement; accomplishment; representation by action.

perfume.e: Borrowed from Middle French parfum, perfum.
perfume.g: A pleasant smell; the scent, odor, or odoriferous particles emitted from a sweet-smelling substance; a pleasant odor.

perfumed.g: Scented, having been given a pleasant smell.

perfumer.e: From perfume (noun and verb) + -er, perhaps modelled on Middle French parfumeur.
perfumer.g: A person who makes or sells perfume.

perhaps.e: From Middle English perhappes, perhappous, variant of earlier perhap (“perhaps, possibly”), equivalent to per- + hap (“chance, coincidence”) + -s, on model of Middle English parchaunce (modern perchance).

peril.e: From Middle English peril, from Old French peril, from Latin perīculum.
peril.g: A situation of serious and immediate danger.

perilous.e: From Middle English perilous, from Old French perilleus, equivalent to peril + -ous, from the noun peril, or from Latin perīculōsus.

perimeter.e: From Latin perimetros, Ancient Greek περίμετρος (perímetros). Equivalent to peri- + meter.
perimeter.g: The sum of the distance of all the lengths of the sides of an object.

period.e: From Middle English periode, from Middle French periode, from Medieval Latin periodus, from Ancient Greek περίοδος (períodos, “circuit, orbit, a recurring interval of time, path around”), from περι- (peri-, “around”) + ὁδός (hodós, “way”).

perish.e: From Middle English perishen, borrowed from Old French perir (via the stem periss- used in various conjugations), from Latin perīre (“pass away, perish”), from per (“through”) + īre (“pass, go”).
perish.g: To decay and disappear; to waste away to nothing.

perishable.e: From Middle English *persishable, perysabyl, equivalent to perish + -able.
perishable.g: Liable to perish, especially naturally subject to quick decomposition or decay.

perjure.e: From Old French parjurer, from Latin periūrō.
perjure.g: To knowingly and willfully make a false statement of witness while in court.

perjury.e: From Anglo-Norman perjurie, from Latin perjūrāre (“swear falsely”), from per- + jūrāre.
perjury.g: The deliberate giving of false or misleading testimony under oath.

permanent.e: From Middle English permanent, permanente, from Middle French permanent, from Latin permanēns, from permaneō (“to stay through”).

permanently.e: From Middle English permanently; equivalent to permanent + -ly.

permissible.e: From Middle English permyssyble, from Old French permissible, from Medieval Latin permissibilis.

permission.e: From Middle English permision, permission, permissioun, permyssion, from Middle French permission, from Latin permissiō. Equivalent to permit + -ion. Mostly replaced native English leave, from Old English lēaf (“permission”).
permission.g: authorisation; consent (especially formal consent from someone in authority)

permit.e: From Middle English permitten, borrowed from Middle French permettre, from Latin permittō (“give up, allow”), from per (“through”) + mittō (“send”).
permit.g: To allow (something) to happen, to give permission for.

permit.e: An irregular borrowing from Spanish palometa, probably from a Doric variant of Ancient Greek πηλαμύς (pēlamús, “young tuna”).
permit.g: A pompano of the species Trachinotus falcatus.

pernicious.e: From Middle English, from Old French pernicios, from Latin perniciōsus (“destructive”), from perniciēs (“destruction”), from per (“through”) + nex (“slaughter, death”).
pernicious.g: Causing much harm in a subtle way.

perpetual.e: From Middle English perpetuel, from Old French perpetuel, from Latin perpetuālis (“universal”), from perpetuus, from petō.
perpetual.g: Lasting forever, or for an indefinitely long time.

perpetually.e: From Middle English perpetuelly; equivalent to perpetual + -ly.
perpetually.g: Seeming to never end; endlessly; constantly.

perplex.e: From Old French, from Latin perplexus (“entangled, confused”), from per (“through”) + plexus, perfect passive participle of plectō (“plait, weave, braid”).
perplex.g: To cause to feel baffled; to puzzle.

perplexity.e: From Middle English perplexite, borrowed from Middle French perplexité or post-classical Latin perplexitās, from perplexus (“entangled”). By surface analysis, perplex + -ity.
perplexity.g: The state or quality of being perplexed.

persecute.e: Borrowed from Middle French persécuter, from Ecclesiastical Latin persecutor, from Latin persequor, persecutus (“follow up, pursue”), from per- (“through”) + sequor (“follow”) (English sequel).
persecute.g: To pursue in a manner to do harm or cruelty to; especially, because of the victim's race, sexual identity, or adherence to a particular beli

persecution.e: Equivalent to persecute + -ion. From Middle English persecucioun, from Old French persecucion, from Ecclesiastical Latin persecūtio (“persecution; chase, pursuit”), from Latin persequor (“follow up, pursue”), from per- (“through”) + sequor (“follow”).
persecution.g: The act of persecuting, especially a specific group of people; an instance of persecution.

persecutor.e: From Middle English persecutour, from Old French persecutor and Latin persecūtor.
persecutor.g: A person or thing that persecutes or harasses.

perseverance.e: From Middle English perseveraunce, from Old French perseverance, from Latin persevērantia.
perseverance.g: Continuing in a course of action without regard to discouragement, opposition or previous failure.

persevere.e: From Middle English perseveren, from Old French perseverer, from Latin persevērāre (“to continue steadfastly, persist, persevere”), from perseverus (“very strict or earnest”), from per (“through, by the means of”) + severus (“strict, earnest”).
persevere.g: To persist steadfastly in pursuit of an undertaking, task, journey, or goal, even if hindered by distraction, difficulty, obstacles, or disc

persist.e: From Middle French persister (Modern French persister), from Latin persistere, from per- + sistere (“to stand”).
persist.g: To go on stubbornly or resolutely.

persistence.e: From Middle French persistance, from persistant, from Latin persistēns, from persistō. By surface analysis, persist + -ence.

persistent.e: From Latin persistentem, present participle of persistō (“continue steadfastly”). By surface analysis, persist + -ent.
persistent.g: Obstinately refusing to give up or let go.

person.e: From Middle English persoun, personne et al., from Anglo-Norman parsone, persoun et al. (Old French persone (“human being”), French personne), and its source Latin persōna (“mask used by actor; role, part, character”), perhaps a loanword from Etruscan 𐌘𐌄𐌓𐌔𐌖 (φersu, “mask”).
person.g: An individual who has been granted personhood; usually a human being.

personal.e: From Middle English personal, personele, from Anglo-Norman personel, personal, personell, Old French personal, personel, from Late Latin persōnālis (“of a person, personly”), equivalent to person + -al.
personal.g: Pertaining to persons (human beings as opposed to things or animals).

personally.e: From Middle English personally, personely, personallich, personaliche, equivalent to personal + -ly.

perspective.e: From Middle English perspective, perspectif, attested since 1381, from Old French or Middle French, from the first word of the Medieval Latin perspectiva ars (“science of optics”), the feminine of Latin perspectivus (“of sight, optical”).

perspire.e: Borrowed from Middle French perspirer and its source Latin perspīrō (“to breathe everywhere, blow constantly”), from per (“through”) + spīrō (“to breathe”); see spirit.
perspire.g: To emit (sweat or perspiration) through the skin's pores.

persuade.g: To successfully convince (someone) to agree to, accept, or do something, usually through reasoning and verbal influence.

persuasion.e: From French persuasion and its source, Latin persuāsiō, from persuādēre, from suādēre (“to advise, recommend”).
persuasion.g: The act of persuading, or trying to do so; the addressing of arguments to someone with the intention of changing their mind or convincing th

persuasive.e: From Middle French persuasif, from Medieval Latin persuāsīvus, from Latin past participle stem of persuādēre + -īvus.

persuasiveness.g: The capability of a person or argument to convince or persuade someone to accept a desired way of thinking.

pertain.e: From Middle English pertenen, from Old French partenir, pertenir (modern French appartenir), in turn from Latin pertineō, pertinēre.
pertain.g: To belong to or be connected as a part, adjunct, attribute, or accessory.

pervade.g: To be in every part of; to spread through; to permeate.

perverse.e: From Middle English perverse, pervers, from Old French pervers, from Latin perversum (“thoroughly turned”), past participle of pervertere, from per- (“thoroughly”) + vertere (“to turn”).
perverse.g: Turned aside while against something, splitting off from a thing.

perversion.g: The action of perverting someone or something; humiliation; debasement.

perversity.e: From perverse + -ity, from Middle French perversité, from Latin perversitās.

pervert.e: From Old French pervertir, itself from the Latin pervertō.
pervert.g: One who has been perverted; one who has turned to error, or adopted a twisted sense of values or morals.

pester.e: The modern sense is an extension of the sense “infest”. Comparable to English construction pest + -er (used to form frequentative verbs).
pester.g: To bother, harass, or annoy persistently.

pestilence.e: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin pestilentia (“plague”), from pestilens (“infected, unwholesome, noxious”); equivalent to pestilent + -ence.
pestilence.g: Any epidemic disease that is highly contagious, infectious, virulent and devastating.

pestilent.e: Middle English, from Latin pestilens, from Latin pestis.
pestilent.g: Highly injurious or destructive to life: deadly.

pestle.e: From Middle English pestel, pestell, from Old French pestel, from Latin pistillum, from pīnsō (“pound, beat”).
pestle.g: A club-shaped, round-headed stick used in a mortar to pound, crush, rub or grind things.

pet.e: Originally northern dialectal, from Scots pet (“an animal that has been tamed and is kept as a pet; a darling or favourite; a petted or spoiled child”), probably from Scottish Gaelic peata (“pet, tamed animal, spoiled child”), from Middle Irish petta, peta (“pet, lap-dog”), of uncertain origin, possibly from a pre-Indo-European substrate.
pet.g: An animal kept as a companion or otherwise for pleasure, rather than for some practical benefit or use.
A fit of petulance, a sulk, arising from the impression that one has been offended or slighted.

petal.e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek πέταλον (pétalon), from πέταλος (pétalos, “broad, flat”), from Proto-Hellenic *pétalos, from Proto-Indo-European *peth₂- (“to spread out”), whence Latin pandō and Proto-Germanic *faþmaz (“embrace”) (English fathom).
petal.g: One of the component parts of the corolla of a flower. It applies particularly, but not necessarily only, when the corolla consists of separ

petition.e: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French peticiun, from stem of Latin petitio, petitionem (“a request, solicitation”), from petere (“to require, seek, go forward”).
petition.g: A formal written request made by an individual or a group of people to a sovereign or political authority, often containing many signatures,
